subject: Ursa Minor
hook: URSA MINOR IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK
angle: Ursa Minor was not always a guide for the North Star, as Polaris was not the true celestial pole star until the modern era; in classical antiquity, the constellation was used for navigation because the celestial pole was closer to a different star, Beta Ursae Minoris.
angle_support: In classical antiquity, the celestial pole was somewhat closer to Beta Ursae Minoris than to Alpha Ursae Minoris, and the entire constellation was taken to indicate the northern direction.

Since the medieval period, it has become convenient to use Alpha Ursae Minoris (or "Polaris") as the North Star. (Even though, in the medieval period, Polaris was still several degrees away from the celestial pole.)
title: Why Polaris wasn't always the North Star
description: While we associate Ursa Minor exclusively with Polaris today, ancient mariners navigated by different stars. The celestial pole has moved over millennia, changing which star pointed the way.
narration: URSA MINOR IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK You picture Polaris as the ancient beacon for every sailor. It was closer to Beta Ursae Minoris, which served as the true reference for early navigators instead. During classical antiquity, the celestial pole was situated significantly closer to Kochab, or Beta Ursae Minoris. Ancient mariners relied on the entire constellation's position to mark north, long before Polaris earned its modern title as the pole star. The true northern guide has shifted across the long night sky.
